title: The upgrade that wasn't
intro: An investor pays a SIF's ₹10L entry for the long-short 'smoother ride'. A year later, was the upgrade real? Open the evidence.

facts.label: The monthly grid
facts.value: Against the Nifty 500, most SIFs and the index barely diverge for most of the year — green and red months track the market.

facts.label: March–April 2026
facts.value: The market breaks. This is the first genuine test of the short book — and the only stretch where funds separate.

facts.label: The one protector
facts.value: A single equity long-short SIF cushioned the fall first and chased the rally second — the promise, delivered.

facts.label: The rest
facts.value: Peers 'barely cushioned at all'. One gave little protection but rode the rebound to finish ahead anyway.

facts.label: The mechanics
facts.value: Shorting requires conviction and being visibly wrong repeatedly. The category's earliest funds aren't a year old.

question: What's the honest reading of SIF year one?
choices: Long-short doesn't work — the category should be avoided
Most managers barely used the shorting freedom, so early returns aren't a verdict on it — judge by the months that test the short book
All SIFs protected well in the crash
SIFs are identical to index funds and always will be
debrief: The grid's story is behavioral, not structural: most months show index-hugging because most managers aren't running meaningful short books — and one manager who did delivered exactly the promised shape (protect first, chase second). So year one is a verdict on usage, not on the strategy: the tools work when spent; most won't spend them. The transferable rule: when you pay for a mandate freedom — shorting, duration flexibility, going anywhere — audit whether it's exercised, and judge it on the periods designed to test it.
